# Boundaries that hold {#sec-shape}

Good architecture is divide and conquer. Give each concern a home, then make the
dependencies point one way. A small application stays easy to change; a larger one stays
possible to test.

## QML composes, C++ owns state {#sec-split}

QML is where a person sees and acts. C++ owns state, rules, files, and work that must outlive
a view. This split helps whenever a UI changes faster than its behaviour. Sketchbook's canvas
binds a button to C++ state and sends an action back to the store.

::: {.snippet source="src/canvas/CanvasPage.qml"}

```qml
                ToolButton {\n                    icon.source: Theme.icon("undo-2")
                    onClicked: root.store.undo()\n                }
```

:::

The store exposes a narrow, typed surface. QML can observe it and call its actions, but it
does not reach into a sketch or mutate it directly.

The following adapted example keeps only the members used above. The complete class is in
[CanvasStore.hpp](https://github.com/deeedob/qt-kickstart/blob/main/src/canvas/CanvasStore.hpp).

```cpp
class CanvasStore : public QObject
{
    Q_OBJECT
    Q_PROPERTY(bool canUndo READ canUndo NOTIFY changed FINAL)

public:
    bool canUndo() const;
    Q_INVOKABLE void undo();

Q_SIGNALS:
    void changed();
};
```

## Layers divide work {#sec-layers}

Split on a responsibility that changes for a different reason. The view changes with the
interaction. A store or view model changes with application behaviour. Core code changes with
the problem domain. Storage changes with files or services.

| Boundary | Holds | Sketchbook |
|---|---|---|
| View | QML, layout, input | `SketchbookPage.qml` |
| Application | UI-facing state and commands | `SketchbookViewModel` |
| Core | reusable rules and values | `shapes::Recognizer` |
| Backend | files, network, devices | `SketchStorage` |

Each lower layer can work without its caller. That is what makes unit tests small and code
reusable. It also leaves a clear place to look when one concern changes.

## One-way flow {#sec-flow}

Commands go down. State changes come back as signals, then QML bindings redraw. A lower layer
never calls its caller.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant V as CanvasPage
    participant S as CanvasStore
    participant M as SketchbookViewModel
    participant F as SketchStorage
    V->>S: undo()
    S-->>V: changed()
    S-->>M: edited()
    M->>F: save()
```

This is not ceremony. A storage test does not need a window, and a new QML screen does not
need to know how files are written.

## Dependencies enforce the boundary {#sec-direction}

The build helps enforce the rule. Targets declare their dependencies and inherit public usage
requirements, including headers. This is not a security boundary: a target can also add include
directories directly. Keep those declarations aligned with the design. If a lower layer needs
an upward dependency, reconsider the boundary or move a shared value down.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[app] --> SB[sketchbook] --> C[canvas] --> SH[shapes]
    SB --> ST[controls]
    C --> ST
```

The arrows show dependencies between targets, not the order in which signals travel. The
application connects features; the shape recognizer does not depend on the application.

::: {.snippet source="src/canvas/CMakeLists.txt"}

```cmake
target_link_libraries(app_canvas
    PRIVATE app_controls\n)
```

:::

## Interfaces at the seams {#sec-interfaces}

An interface describes what a caller needs without tying it to how the work happens. It helps
at a boundary to a network, device, or clock: production code can use the real service while
a test supplies a predictable implementation. Qt's `QIODevice`, for example, provides a
common interface for files and network sockets.

An interface costs another concept to maintain. Sketchbook's storage tests use temporary
directories, so a separate storage interface would not help them today. Add one when a real
alternative makes the boundary easier to use or test.

## The composition root {#sec-composition-root}

The composition root is where concrete objects are created and connected. In Sketchbook that
place is `main()`: it creates long-lived objects before the QML engine and passes typed inputs
to QML. Their lifetime and dependencies stay visible, and a test can construct the same graph
directly. A larger application can put that wiring in an application manager owned by `main()`;
the important part is keeping the wiring and ownership explicit.

::: {.snippet source="src/app/main.cpp"}

```cpp
    const auto sketchDirectory
    });
```
